Now let me compile the verse-by-verse commentary from all these sources.

---

# Genesis 16 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1: *"Now Abram's wife Sarai had borne him no children, but she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar."*

- **The problem stated.** Despite God's promise of descendants (Gen 12:2; 13:15–16), Sarai remained barren. Moses sets this up as the point of departure for all that follows. The barrenness is the "cause or occasion of the subsequent transaction" (Pulpit Commentary). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Hagar's origin.** Hagar was almost certainly acquired during Abram's sojourn in Egypt (Gen 12:16). Spurgeon notes: "If Abraham had lived the separated life, and had not fallen into the customs of those round about him, he would not have had that sin and sorrow concerning Hagar" (quoted in Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Name meaning.** "Hagar" is related to the Hebrew root for "flight" (cf. the Islamic *Hegirah*). It may be a name given after her flight, not her original designation (Pulpit, citing Ambrose, Wordsworth, Michaelis, Bush). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Precept Austin** notes: not once in vv. 1–6 do Sarai or Abram consult God. "That generally bodes ill for what follows!" Abram was living as "exalted father" in name only. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]
- **Matthew Henry** observes that Hagar was "an obscure Egyptian woman, whose name and story we never should have heard of if Providence had not brought her into the family of Abram." [https://www.ccel.org/h/henry/mhc2/MHC01016.HTM]

## v. 2: *"So Sarai said to Abram, 'Look now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her.' And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai."*

- **Sarai's theology was accurate but her faith was faltering.** She rightly recognised God's sovereignty over the womb ("the LORD has prevented me"), but her statement is "more of a complaint than a humble recognition of and trust in the Creator's promise" (Ligonier/Reformed). [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sarai-took-hagar]
- **"Perhaps I can build a family by her."** Literally "be built up by her" — from *banah*, to build, whence *ben*, a son (Pulpit). The proposal was culturally accepted in the ancient Near East: a barren wife could give her servant as a surrogate; the child would legally belong to the wife. The Nuzi tablets attest to this Hurrian custom (Precept Austin, citing Bob Utley). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]
- **Calvin's nuanced view:** The Pulpit Commentary cites Calvin — Sarai's desire was not merely natural impulse but "the zeal of faith which made her wish to secure the promised benediction," since it had not yet been clearly revealed that *Sarai* would be the mother. Yet "the faith of both was defective; not indeed with regard to the substance of the promise, but with regard to the method in which they proceeded." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **"Abram listened to the voice of Sarai."** This Hebrew phrase ("listened to the voice of") is identical to Gen 3:17, where God chastises Adam: "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife..." Ligonier highlights this as deliberate parallelism by Moses: "Genesis 16 is a re-run of Genesis 3! A fall takes place in the life of the great patriarch." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/voices-of-temptation] (from search snippet). Also [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sarai-took-hagar]
- **Matthew Henry:** "It is the policy of Satan to tempt us by our nearest and dearest relations… Foul temptations may have very fair pretenses, and be coloured with that which is very plausible." Abram married without God's consent: "This persuasion came not of him that called him." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** Sarai's pain was real — deferred hope, unanswered prayers, empty arms, public shame — but it led her into the sin of unbelief. "Abram should have said… 'Sarai, bless your heart – but you're my wife and we're in this together. Difficult as it is, let's believe God all over again for a miracle.'" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Desiring God (John Piper):** "Abraham and Sarah weaken in their faith for a time and devise a plan by which they will use their own resources to help God fulfill his promise." Ishmael was born "according to the flesh" — the product of self-reliance rather than trusting God's supernatural power. (From search snippet) [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/hagar-and-slavery-vs-sarah-and-freedom]

## v. 3: *"So after he had lived in Canaan for ten years, his wife Sarai took her Egyptian maidservant Hagar and gave her to Abram to be his wife."*

- **Ten years of waiting.** Abram would have been about 85 and Sarai 75. The time note "probably accounts for their impatience" (Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **"To be his wife."** The Pulpit Commentary notes she is more properly a *pilgash* (concubine), later styled as such in Gen 25:6. The term "wife" here is "improper," since the concubine differed from a true wife in family authority, manner of espousal, and inheritance rights of offspring. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** "Abram did not actually marry Hagar, but he acted towards her as a man should only act towards his wife." The whole arrangement was against God's plan for marriage (one man, one woman, one flesh). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Ligonier** notes that Abram's earlier sojourn in Egypt (Gen 12:10–20) "should have told him that God intended to provide his heir from Sarai's loins." Right after the visible confirmation of the covenant in chapter 15, Abram yields to this suggestion. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/sarai-took-hagar]

## v. 4: *"And he slept with Hagar, and she conceived. But when Hagar realized that she was pregnant, she began to despise her mistress."*

- **Immediate conception** suggested to all involved that the infertility problem lay with Sarai, not Abram. In a culture that prized childbearing, this gave the servant Hagar greater status and made her "appear more blessed than Sarai" (Enduring Word). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **"Her mistress was despised in her eyes."** The Pulpit Commentary notes that barrenness among the Hebrews was a dishonour and reproach (1 Sam 1:6; Gen 30:1, 23), while fecundity was a special mark of divine favour. Hagar, "immediately on perceiving her condition, became insolent" (cf. Prov 30:23). Whether she imagined Sarai was rejected by God or anticipated displacing Sarai as Abram's wife, her pride was immediate. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** "Hagar immediately began to think of herself as better and greater than Sarai. A bad situation became worse." Results don't justify sin: "Whatever a man or woman attempts to do without God will be a miserable failure – or an even more miserable success." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **A Reformed note (Ligonier):** "Despite her sinful pride, Yahweh did not abandon Hagar" — this anticipates the grace shown in vv. 7ff. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-has-listened] (from search snippet)

## v. 5: *"Then Sarai said to Abram, 'May the wrong done to me be upon you! I delivered my servant into your arms, and ever since she saw that she was pregnant, she has treated me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me.'"*

- **"My wrong be upon thee."** The Pulpit Commentary surveys interpretations: "thou art the cause of it" (Jonathan, Rosenmüller); "it belongs to thee as well as to me" (Clericus, Bush); or, perhaps best, "May the injury done to me return upon thee!" (Keil, Kalisch, Lange, Wordsworth) — "the language of passionate irritation, indicating repentance of her previous action." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Calvin** calls her appeal "an irreverent use of the Divine name" and Ainsworth calls it "a speech arguing great passion" (Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** Sarai blamed the whole situation on Abram, "and there was some reason for this. Abram should have acted as the spiritual leader." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Ligonier ("Voices of Temptation"):** "Just like Eden (where Eve blames the serpent, and Adam blames Eve) this tale, too, is a tennis match of counter culpability. Sarai, who had first suggested the idea, is filled with envy… and thrashes out at Abram." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/voices-of-temptation] (from search snippet)

## v. 6: *"'Here,' said Abram, 'your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her.' Then Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that she fled from her."*

- **Abram's abdication.** The Pulpit Commentary notes multiple interpretations of Abram's conduct: (1) evidence of his peaceful disposition — doing violence to his own feelings as a husband to restore household harmony (Calvin); (2) proof he had already realised his mistake in expecting the promised seed through Hagar (Calvin); (3) weakness in yielding to Sarai's passionate invective (Willet, Bush); (4) an unjustifiable wrong inflicted on the mother of his child (Candlish). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** "Abram seemed to make a bad situation worse by turning the situation over to Sarai and not taking care of the child he was father to. Yet in this, he also put his relationship with Sarai first, and that was good." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Sarai "dealt harshly"** — literally "afflicted her." Commentators debate whether this means demoting her back to slave status (Lange, Candlish) or physical maltreatment such as beatings (Ainsworth, Bush). Either way, the affliction drove Hagar to flee (Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Precept Austin:** Sarai's "untamed temper" and Hagar's "defiant will" collide — a picture of what happens when we "try to play God." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]

## v. 7: *"Now the angel of the LORD found Hagar by a spring of water in the desert—the spring along the road to Shur."*

- **The Angel of the LORD.** The Pulpit Commentary provides an extended discussion. Some (Augustine, Origen, Jerome, later scholars like Delitzsch, Kurtz) held this was a created angel. But the stronger view (the Fathers, the Reformers, Hengstenberg, Keil, Lange, Ainsworth, Bush, Wordsworth, Candlish) identifies the Angel of the LORD as the Divine Being himself — the pre-incarnate Second Person of the Trinity — because: (1) He explicitly identifies Himself with Jehovah (v. 10) and Elohim (Gen 22:12); (2) those who meet Him recognise Him as divine (v. 13); (3) Biblical writers speak of Him as Jehovah without reserve; (4) this fits earlier foreshadowings of plurality in the Godhead (Gen 1:26; 11:7); (5) the organic unity of Scripture would be broken if the central OT revelation were a mere creature angel while the NT centres on the incarnation of the God-Man. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** "This is the first appearance of the Angel of the LORD in the Bible. He didn't first appear to Noah, Enoch, or Abram. The Angel of the LORD first appeared to a single mother-to-be who had a pride problem and was mistreated by the woman who put her into the whole mess." Guzik identifies this as a pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Ligonier (Reformed)** agrees: "After seeing the angel, Hagar addresses him as God (Gen. 16:13)." While the NT does not explicitly identify the Angel of the LORD with the Son of God, the identification is strongly implied. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/angel-lord] (from search snippet)
- **The road to Shur:** Hagar was heading toward Egypt, her homeland. The spring was a known watering place in the desert of Arabia Deserta, probably the modern *Dachifar* (Pulpit, citing several geographers). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]

## v. 8: *"'Hagar, servant of Sarai,' he said, 'where have you come from, and where are you going?' 'I am running away from my mistress Sarai,' she replied."*

- **"Hagar, Sarai's maid."** The Angel pointedly declines to recognise her marriage to Abram, reminding her of her original position as a bondwoman, "from which liberty was not to be obtained by flight, but by manumission" (Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **The two questions.** Enduring Word: "Where have you come from, and where are you going?" — an important and insightful question. Hagar had acted without thinking about either. "Remembering those two questions and the answers to them would save God's people from a lot of trouble." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Hagar's honest answer** "testifies to the oppression she had experienced, but also to the voice of her own conscience" (Lange, cited in Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]

## v. 9: *"So the angel of the LORD told her, 'Return to your mistress and submit to her authority.'"*

- **A hard command.** The Pulpit Commentary compares this to Paul's instruction to Onesimus, the runaway slave of Philemon. The Hebrew verb for "submit" is the same one used to describe Sarai's harsh treatment of Hagar in v. 6 — meaning Hagar is to "meekly resign herself to the ungracious and oppressive treatment of her mistress." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** "The Angel of the LORD told her to repent. If she changed her direction, there was an inherent promise – 'Obey Me and I will protect you.' The pre-incarnate Jesus didn't exactly tell Hagar to go back to an abusive household; He made an implied promise of protection." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]

## v. 10: *"Then the angel added, 'I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count.'"*

- **"I will greatly multiply."** The language — "multiplying I will multiply" — is language "altogether inappropriate in the lips of a creature" (Pulpit), further evidence that the speaker is divine. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** God gave "a clear promise of staggering blessing. The unborn son of Hagar would be the father of uncountable descendants." Ishmael became the ancestor of the Arab peoples. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Ligonier:** "Though we might have expected Him to chastise her, God does not do so. Instead He tells her to return to Sarai and at the same time promises to bless her with many offspring." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-has-listened] (from search snippet)

## v. 11: *"The angel of the LORD proceeded: 'Behold, you have conceived and will bear a son. And you shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction.'"*

- **Ishmael = "God hears."** This is the first instance in Scripture of a child being named before birth (cf. later Isaac, Josiah, John the Baptist, Jesus) (Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** "Ishmael was given a great promise, not only in the number of his descendants, but also in that he was the first one in the Bible given his name before he was born. God had a plan for this boy." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Ligonier:** "For the rest of her life Hagar will be able to look upon her son and remember how the Lord visited her in her time of need." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-has-listened] (from search snippet)

## v. 12: *"He will be a wild donkey of a man, and his hand will be against everyone, and everyone's hand against him; he will live in hostility toward all his brothers."*

- **"A wild donkey of a man."** The Hebrew *pere'* (wild ass) depicts the Bedouin's "boundless love of freedom… hardy, frugal, reveling in the varied beauty of nature, and despising town life in every form" (Keil, cited in Pulpit). Just as Israel is later called "sheep men" (Ezek 36:37–38), Ishmael's line are "wild ass men." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Prophetic accuracy.** The Pulpit Commentary: "The Arabs of today are 'just as they were described by the spirit of prophecy nearly 4000 years ago'" (quoting Porter's *Giant Cities of Bashan*). Their hand has been against every man for over thirty centuries. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Ligonier:** The wild donkey metaphor is "tellingly used elsewhere in Scripture of those who embrace stubborn autonomy and defy God's covenant (Jer. 2:23–24; Hos. 8:8–9)." The verse signals that Ishmael "will not be the son of promise but will antagonize those who serve the one, true God." The blessing is a mixed one — it will also serve as a reminder of "the consequences that come when man attempts to bring about the Lord's will in ways not sanctioned by Him." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lord-has-listened] (from search snippet)
- **Enduring Word:** The ill effect described "has been mostly seen in violence and murder among Arabs themselves. They kill each other even more than they kill Jews and Christians." Guzik urges prayer for revival among the Arab peoples. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]

## v. 13: *"So Hagar gave this name to the LORD who had spoken to her: 'You are the God who sees me,' for she said, 'Here I have seen the One who sees me!'"*

- **El Roi — "the God who sees me."** The Pulpit Commentary notes two possible meanings: "the God of my vision" (who reveals Himself in vision) or "the God who sees all things, and therefore me." The LXX and Vulgate favour the latter; most Reformers also. Hagar clearly recognised that this was no mere angel — she gave a divine name to the One who spoke to her, "thus identifying the Maleach Jehovah with Jehovah himself." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **"Have I also here seen Him who sees me?"** The more literal rendering: "Have I also hitherto seen?" i.e., "Do I also still live after the vision?" (Gesenius, Keil, Kalisch, Rosenmüller). In the ancient world, seeing God was considered fatal; Hagar marvels that she survived. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word:** "After meeting with El Roi… Hagar knew that if God could be with her in the wilderness, He would be with her in having to submit to Sarai also. It was as if Hagar said to God, 'You have looked upon me, and now I can look upon You.' That face-to-face relationship with God transforms." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Precept Austin** (citing Ligonier's Ligon Duncan): "The idea of God 'seeing' in the Old Testament is identical with the idea of God 'caring.' If He sees, then He cares." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]

## v. 14: *"Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi. It is located between Kadesh and Bered."*

- **"Beer-lahai-roi"** — the Pulpit Commentary gives three possible meanings: (1) "the well of the living one of vision" (of God who appeared there); (2) "the well of the life of vision" (where after seeing God, life was preserved); or (3) "where in consequence of seeing God, a new life was imparted" (Inglis). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- The well's location "between Kadesh and Bered" situates it south of Beersheba, possibly at *Ain Kades* (called *Moilahi Hagar* by Arabs), about twelve miles from Kadesh (Pulpit, citing Keil). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]

## v. 15: *"And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne."*

- **Hagar returned.** Enduring Word: "Apparently, Hagar did return with a submitted heart. She told the whole story to Abram and Sarai, and Abram named the child Ishmael, just as instructed in the meeting with the Angel of the LORD Hagar described." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Abram named the son** — "thus acknowledging the truth of Hagar's vision" (Pulpit). Though the naming by the father is usually assigned to the Elohist source, this chapter is typically held to be Jehovistic, showing the complexity of source-critical theories (Pulpit). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word** adds: "Hagar might have said when she returned, 'I fled from you all because I was so miserable and thought I could not continue here. But the Lord met me and told me He would see me through. He told me to come back and submit to you, so that is why I'm here.'" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]

## v. 16: *"Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him."*

- **The timeline.** Abram was 75 when he left Haran (Gen 12:4). After ten years in Canaan (v. 3), he is now 86. It would be another 14 years before Isaac, the child of promise, was born (Gen 21:5 — Abram was 100). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Enduring Word** connects this to the long wait that still lay ahead: "Even after this, it would still be more than 13 years until the child of promise came. When a believer impatiently tries to fulfill God's promises in their own effort, it accomplishes nothing and may even prolong the time until the promise is fulfilled." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Presbyterian

- **Genesis 16 as a "re-run of the Fall."** Ligonier (and many Reformed commentators) emphasises the deliberate literary parallel between Gen 3 and Gen 16: the identical Hebrew wording for "listened to the voice of," the women seizing initiative, the men passively following. "Moses intends for us to see that Genesis 16 is a re-run of Genesis 3! A fall takes place in the life of the great patriarch." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/voices-of-temptation]
- **The Angel of the LORD as pre-incarnate Christ.** Reformed teachers strongly identify the Angel as the Second Person of the Trinity. Ligonier states: "After seeing the angel, Hagar addresses him as God (Gen. 16:13)." While noting the NT does not explicitly identify the Angel with the Son, the implication is upheld. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/angel-lord]
- **Sovereignty and waiting.** Reformed teaching stresses that God's delay was purposeful — to stretch faith, magnify grace, and ensure that the fulfilment would be unmistakably supernatural. "God often shapes the details of our lives into stories that cause our faith to be stretched." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/waiting-on-god]

### Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)

- **"The Isaac Factor"** — Piper teaches that God deliberately makes His promises humanly impossible so that we must trust His power and He gets the glory. Ishmael was born "according to the flesh" (self-reliance); Isaac "through promise" (supernatural intervention). "Ishmael was not the son of promise, precisely because he was humanly possible." [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-isaac-factor]
- **Allegory of two covenants** (Gal 4:21–31). Piper teaches that Hagar represents the covenant from Mount Sinai — slavery, self-effort, "present Jerusalem." Sarah represents the Jerusalem above — freedom, grace, promise. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/hagar-and-slavery-vs-sarah-and-freedom]

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

- **Emphasis on personal encounter.** Guzik stresses that Hagar's transformation came "not from changing her circumstances but from a face-to-face encounter with God that changed her heart." Application focuses on the experiential: "If you must submit in difficult circumstances, God sees. If you ache under the pain of ministry, God sees. If you just feel like running, God sees." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **Prayer for the Arab peoples.** Guzik uniquely draws application toward revival: "We may take this as a prompting to pray for revival and spiritual awakening among the Arab peoples, because when they cry out to Jesus, God will hear." He notes that "angelic visitations and visitations of Jesus continue to this day among the descendants of Ishmael." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]
- **First appearance to the unlikely.** Guzik highlights that the Angel of the LORD's *first* biblical appearance was not to a patriarch but "to a pregnant servant woman with a pride problem — a stunning reminder of God's love for the unlikely." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-16/]

### Evangelical (Precept Austin)

- **"Don't give in to presumption and passivity."** The summary by Paul Apple captures the broadly evangelical application: Sarai's scheming = playing God (presumption); Abram's failure to lead = passivity. "Whenever we try to play God, we make a mess of things, but God can show mercy." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]
- **Satanic attempts to thwart the Messianic line.** Bob Utley places the birth of Ishmael in a list of Satanic attacks on the Messianic seed, alongside Cain's murder of Abel, the Nephilim, the Tower of Babel, Abram giving Sarai to Pharaoh, and later to Abimelech. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]

---

## Other Views

### Modern / Critical Scholarship (NET Bible notes, via Precept Austin)

- **Social custom background.** The NET Bible notes that Sarai's proposal "simply sees this as the social custom of having a child through a surrogate." The Hebrew term *shifkhah* ("maidservant") refers to a menial female servant; the story "illustrates the limits of Abram's faith as he tries to obtain a son through social custom." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]
- **Source criticism.** The Pulpit Commentary notes (and rejects) the hypothesis that repetitions in vv. 1–3 require different authorship (Tuch, Colenso, Bleek, Davidson). It argues these repetitions are "characteristic of the genius of Hebrew composition." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/16.htm]
- **Nuzi tablets.** Bob Utley (via Precept Austin) notes that the practice of surrogate motherhood through a servant is "very much in line with the Nuzi Tablets which describe the Hurrian culture of the second millennium B.C." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-16-commentary]

### Catholic / Orthodox readings

- No results were found in my searches from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org that provide distinct Catholic or Orthodox verse-by-verse commentary on this chapter. The Pulpit Commentary (biblehub.com) cites some Church Fathers (Ambrose on Hagar's name; Augustine, Origen, Jerome on the Angel of the LORD), but their views are integrated into the main commentary tradition rather than representing a distinctly Catholic interpretation today.
- The Catholic tradition typically reads this passage in light of Galatians 4:21–31 (the allegory of Hagar = the Old Covenant, Sarah = the New Covenant), consistent with the broader Protestant understanding.

### Debated Popular Modern Teachings

- No prosperity gospel, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace readings of this chapter surfaced in my searches from the permitted domains. The chapter's emphasis on the painful consequences of fleshly self-effort and the command to "return and submit" runs counter to typical prosperity or hyper-grace emphases.
